target_customer: Teens and young adults who share a daily self photo with friends
problem: Social updates were mostly text; DailyBooth let people keep friends updated through a photo a day with a caption.
business_model: Free social network, advertising intended; no revenue figures found

founders.name: Ryan Amos
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page; Wikipedia calls him lead developer. No background found.

founders.name: Jon Wheatley
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page. No background found.

exit.reason: Talent acquisition; the team joined Airbnb and the DailyBooth site was shut by 2012-12-31. The company's user email gave no concrete reason.

technical_complexity.rationale: Photo upload, follow graph and comments on standard web stack; scaling to millions of photos was the main work.

defensibility.rationale: Teen audience and celebrity followers gave some network effect, but photo feeds were easy to copy and Instagram arrived later.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Facebook and Twitter owned the status update and photo habit; Instagram later captured mobile photo sharing. DailyBooth ended as an Airbnb talent acquisition.

market_need_then: Photo blogging and status update following were growing in 2009, and the site passed 1,000,000 photos on 2009-09-07 and 3,000,000 photos in early 2010 per Wikipedia.

branding.domain_note: Used dailybooth.com; no purchase history found. The domain no longer resolves from this environment.

identity.voice_and_tone: Slogan was your life in pictures.

branding.brand_signature: Photo booth unit of content called a booth, compared by the CEO to a tweet.
branding.community_and_virality: Celebrities such as Ashton Kutcher and Demi Moore joined and brought followers; the user base skewed to teens.

brand_strength.rationale: Clear, descriptive name tied to the format and strong teen and celebrity attention, but short lived. Reportedly YC considered a name change but feared a community revolt.

outcome_analysis: DailyBooth launched in February 2009, grew fast with teens and celebrity users, raised about 7 million dollars from Sequoia, Ignition and angels, and was bought by Airbnb in a talent deal in 2012, then closed on 2012-12-31. The company gave no concrete reason for the closure. Instagram and the mobile photo wave overshadowed it, so the team landed softly rather than continuing the product, though the cause is not stated by the company.
notes: Competitors dated 2009 were not found beyond generic CB Insights lists, so the list is empty. Total raised is listed as $7.02M over 5 rounds by CB Insights. The Airbnb deal is dated April 2012 by Wikipedia and the shutdown email was reported in October and November 2012; Airbnb's price is not public. The acquirer's role of the Batch CEO is mentioned by one outlet; he is not on the YC founder list so not recorded. Founder education and prior employers not found.
